1. Introduction 
STEM education has become a central component of educational and economic policy because 
scientific and technological capabilities are associated with innovation, productivity, industrial 
development, and social problem -solving. Across national contexts, g overnments and 
universities increasingly view competence in science, technology, engineering, and 
mathematics as necessary for participation in knowledge-based economies. However, technical 
competence alone does not ensure that scientific ideas, engineerin g designs, or technological 
prototypes become useful innovations. The movement from technical knowledge to social or 
economic value often requires additional capacities related to identifying needs, understanding

regulation, forming teams, communicating value, and developing viable organisational models. 
This concern has contributed to growing interest in entrepreneurial STEM education. 
Entrepreneurial STEM education may be understood as the intentional integration of 
entrepreneurship, innovation, and business principles into STEM learning environments. It does 
not only refer to the creation of startups. It also includes the ability to apply technical knowledge 
in ways that create value within firms, public institutions, research organisations, communities, 
and social enterprises. In this sense, entrepreneu rial STEM education is relevant to students 
who may become founders, engineers, scientists, product developers, educators, public -sector 
innovators, or technology managers. 
The need for such integration has become more visible as economies are reshaped by 
digitalisation, artificial in

The need for such integration has become more visible as economies are reshaped by 
digitalisation, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, energy transition, advanced manufacturing, 
data science, and platform-based services. These domains often require professionals who can 
work across technical, commercial, regulatory, and social boundaries. The World Economic 
Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2023 identifies analytical thinking, creative thinking, 
technological literacy, resilience, flexibility, leadership, a nd social influence among the skills 
associated with changing labour markets (World Economic Forum, 2023). Such findings 
support the view that STEM education should be connected to broader capabilities for 
innovation and enterprise. 
The United States and Nigeria offer useful contexts for examining entrepreneurial STEM 
education because they represent different innovation ecosystem conditions. The United States 
has a mature research and

A comparison between the two countries does not imply that the United States provides a model 
to be transferred directly to Nigeria. Innovation ecosystems are embedded in institutional, 
historical, economic, and policy contexts. Rather, the comparison prov ides a basis for 
examining how entrepreneurial STEM education may be designed differently under different 
ecosystem conditions. It also supports a more context-sensitive understanding of how business 
principles can be incorporated into STEM education in bo th mature and emerging innovation 
environments.

have each developed substantial bodies of literature, the intersection among them remains

The article contributes to scholarship and practice in three ways. It consolidates literature across 
STEM education, entrepreneurship education, and innovation ecosystem studies. It provides a 
comparative discussion of the United States and Nigeria while a voiding a one -directional 
transfer assumption. It also proposes a six -dimensional framework for integrating business 
principles into STEM education across broader educational levels and institutional settings. 
 
2. Conceptual and Theoretical Background 
STEM education refers to teaching and learning in science, technology, engineering, and 
mathematics, either as separate disciplines or through integrated approaches.

fers to teaching and learning in science, technology, engineering, and 
mathematics, either as separate disciplines or through integrated approaches. Integrated STEM 
education often emphasises the use of knowledge across disciplinary bounda ries to address 
authentic problems (Breiner et al., 2012; National Research Council, 2011). It is commonly 
associated with inquiry, modelling, experimentation, mathematical reasoning, technological 
literacy, and design-based problem-solving. 
Entrepreneurship education refers to educational practices that develop entrepreneurial 
knowledge, attitudes, skills, and behaviours. Earlier approaches often treated entrepreneurship 
education as instruction in business planning. More recent approaches em phasise action, 
experimentation, opportunity development, value creation, uncertainty management, and 
learning through practice (Fayolle, 2013; Lackéus , 2015; Neck & Greene, 2011). This shift 
makes entrepreneurship education relevant beyond business

chunks.text:
learning through practice (Fayolle, 2013; Lackéus , 2015; Neck & Greene, 2011). This shift 
makes entrepreneurship education relevant beyond business schools because many 
entrepreneurial processes resemble inquiry, experimentation, and iterative problem -solving, 
which are already familiar to STEM disciplines. 
Entrepreneurial STEM education sits at the intersection of these traditions. It may be defined 
as the integration of business, entrepreneurship, innovation, and commercialisation principles 
into STEM teaching and learning in order to enable learners to tra nslate technical knowledge 
into social, economic, or technological value. It includes but is not limited to venture creation. 
It may also involve innovation within existing organisations, research commercialisation, social

public-sector innovation. 
Several business principles are particularly relevant to STEM education. Opportunity 
recognition helps learners identify unmet needs and problem spaces rather than beginning only 
from available technologies. Customer discovery and user research help studen ts test 
assumptions about users, beneficiaries, buyers, and other stakeholders. Market analysis assists 
students in understanding demand, competition, adoption barriers, pricing, and distribution. 
Business model development helps students examine how innov ations create, deliver, and 
capture value. Financial literacy supports cost estimation, budgeting, funding decisions, and 
resource planning. Intellectual property knowledge is relevant where students develop 
inventions, software, designs, or research outputs. Regulatory and ethical awareness is needed 
in areas such as health technology, biotechnology,

inventions, software, designs, or research outputs. Regulatory and ethical awareness is needed 
in areas such as health technology, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, energy, environmental 
science, and data -driven systems. Leadership, teamwork, and communication are necessary 
because innovation normally occurs through collaboration across technical and non -technical 
domains. 
This review is informed by three theoretical perspectives: human capital theory, entrepreneurial 
mindset theory, and innovation ecosystem theory. Human capital theory argues that education 
develops knowledge and capabilities that increase individual and societal productivity (Becker, 
1964). From this perspective, business-integrated STEM education develops a broader form of 
human capital by combining technical competence with innovation, commercialisation, and 
enterprise-related capabilities. 
Entrepreneurial mindset theory focuses on cognitive and behavioural orientations associated 
with entre

enterprise-related capabilities. 
Entrepreneurial mindset theory focuses on cognitive and behavioural orientations associated 
with entrepreneurial action. These include opportunity recognition, creativity, adaptability, 
resilience, initiative, and the ability to act under uncertainty (Hayn ie et al., 2010; McGrath & 
MacMillan, 2000). In STEM education, the entrepreneurial mindset helps students move from 
solving predefined technical problems to framing open -ended problems, evaluating 
alternatives, working with users, and iterating toward feasible and useful solutions. 
Innovation ecosystem theory explains entrepreneurial outcomes as products of interactions 
among individuals, organisations, policies, resources, networks, and institutions. The Triple 
Helix model emphasises university -industry-government interaction in inn ovation processes 
(Etzkowitz & Leydesdorff, 2000). More recent ecosystem scholarship extends this perspective 
by considering finance, culture,

inn ovation processes 
(Etzkowitz & Leydesdorff, 2000). More recent ecosystem scholarship extends this perspective 
by considering finance, culture, infrastructure, talent, networks, and institutions as parts of 
entrepreneurial environments (Spigel, 2017; Stam, 2015). For entrepreneurial STEM education, 
this means that curriculum reform alone is insufficient. Students require connections to 
laboratories, mentors, industry partners, community users, intellectual property systems, 
incubators, accelerators, investors, and supportive policies. 
Together, these perspectives suggest that entrepreneurial STEM education operates at 
individual, institutional, and ecosystem levels. At the individual level, it develops technical, 
entrepreneurial, and business capabilities. At the institutional level, it  requires curriculum 
design, faculty development, interdisciplinary structures, and practical support systems. At the

ecosystem level, it depends on university -industry-government-community relationships, 
funding structures, policy frameworks, and innovation infrastructure. 
3. Methods 
This article adopts an integrative literature review approach to examine the integration of 
business principles into STEM education, with attention to entrepreneurial STEM education 
and innovation ecosystems in the United States and Nigeria. An integrative  review was 
considered appropriate because the topic spans several bodies of literature, including STEM 
education, entrepreneurship education, engineering education, higher education studies, 
innovation ecosystem research, technology commercialisation, and development policy. Unlike 
a narrow systematic review focused on a single intervention or outcome, an integrative review 
allows theoretical, empirical, and policy sources to be examined together in order to clarify 
concepts, identify patterns, compare contexts, and develop a conceptual framework.

STEM education is conceptualised across relevant literature. The second examined the business 
principles considered relevant to STEM curricula. The third considered pedagogical approaches 
used to support entrepreneurial learning in STEM contexts. The fourth examined institutional, 
policy, and ecosystem factors that enable or constrain implementation. The fifth compared the 
United States and Nigeria as different innovation ecosystem contexts.

The literature was analysed thematically. Initial reading focused on identifying how 
entrepreneurial STEM education was defined, what business principles were discussed, what 
pedagogical approaches were used, and what institutional or ecosystem factors wer e 
emphasised. Sources were then grouped into themes relating to conceptualisation, business 
principles, pedagogy, institutional supports, barriers, comparative context, and policy 
implications. The synthesis was interpretive rather than statistical because  the literature 
included conceptual papers, empirical studies, programme analyses, and policy reports. The 
review therefore aimed to develop a conceptual and comparative framework rather than 
estimate the effect size of a single intervention.

6.1 Conceptualisation of Entrepreneurial STEM Education 
The literature suggests that entrepreneurial STEM education is not a single programme model 
but a family of approaches that connect technical knowledge with value creation. In some 
studies, the concept is framed around venture creation, especially where st udents are expected 
to develop prototypes, business models, and startup ideas. In others, it is framed more broadly 
as innovation capability, employability, or the development of an entrepreneurial mindset. This 
broader interpretation is useful because many STEM graduates will not establish firms but may 
still require entrepreneurial capabilities in research, industry, public service, education, and 
community development. 
Entrepreneurship education scholarship has increasingly moved away from passive instruction 
toward practice -based and action -oriented learning. Neck and Greene (2011) argued that 
entrepreneurship should be taught as a method, involving practice

technology, or laboratory-based discovery. In computing and digital technology, entrepreneurial 
STEM education often appears through software development, platform creation, artificial

The literature also indicates that entrepreneurial STEM education is better understood as a 
developmental process rather than a single course. Learners may first be introduced to

property, customer discovery, business models, a nd venture development. For postgraduate 
students and researchers, entrepreneurial STEM education may focus on technology transfer, 
research commercialisation, licensing, startup formation, and industry collaboration.

6.2 Business Principles Integrated into STEM Education 
The literature identifies several business principles that are relevant to STEM curricula. 
Opportunity recognition is one of the most frequently discussed. STEM students often begin 
with a technical solution, but entrepreneurial education encourages them t o begin with a 
problem, need, or opportunity. This shift is significant because technological novelty does not 
automatically translate into usefulness. Students must learn to ask whether a problem is 
important, who experiences it, what alternatives already  exist, and why a proposed solution 
would be adopted. 
Customer discovery is closely related to opportunity recognition. It involves direct engagement 
with potential users, customers, beneficiaries, or stakeholders. In technology entrepreneurship 
education, customer discovery helps students test assumptio

education, customer discovery helps students test assumptions before committing resources to 
product development. NSF I -Corps is a prominent example of this approach because it trains 
teams to examine whether their research -based innovations address real market or user needs 
(National Science Foundation, n.d.; Nnakwe et al., 2018). 
Market analysis is also central. Students need to understand market size, segmentation, 
competition, pricing, distribution, and adoption barriers. This is not only relevant to commercial 
markets. Social innovations and public -sector technologies also requi re analysis of 
stakeholders, users, institutions, and implementation environments. A water purification 
system, educational technology platform, diagnostic device, or renewable energy solution must

6.3 Pedagogical Approaches 
The reviewed literature supports pedagogies that allow learners to practise entrepreneurship 
rather than only study it. Project-based learning is one of the most frequently used approaches. 
It allows students to work on authentic problems, develop technica l solutions, examine users, 
consider costs, and present implementation strategies. Project -based learning is suitable for 
entrepreneurial STEM education because it permits the integration of technical and business 
decisions within a single learning experience.

Problem-based learning is also relevant because it begins with open-ended problems. Students 
must define the problem, identify what they need to learn, collect information, and develop 
possible solutions. This process mirrors entrepreneurial uncertainty, where problems are often 
ambiguous and solutions must be revised as new information becomes available. 
Design thinking has become influential in innovation education because it emphasises empathy, 
problem framing, ideation, prototyping, testing, and iteration. In STEM education, design 
thinking can help students pay attention to user experience, context, accessibility, and adoption. 
It is particularly useful in health technology, engineering design, digital product development, 
environmental innovation, and community-based STEM projects.

6.4 Institutional Enablers 
The literature indicates that entrepreneurial STEM education requires institutional support. 
Leadership commitment is one enabling factor. Universities that identify entrepreneurship and 
innovation as institutional priorities are more likely to support centres, laboratories, seed funds, 
faculty training, industry partnerships, and interdisciplinary programmes. Without such 
commitment, entrepreneurial initiatives may depend on individual champions and remain 
vulnerable to discontinuity.

incentives are also important because interdisciplinary teaching and entrepreneurship

while entrepreneurship courses may be located in business schools and taught without reference 
to technical fields. This separation may cause entrepreneurship education to appear generic or 
disconnected from STEM students’ projects and career pathways.

requirements, leaving limited space for new content

7.1 United States 
The United States has a developed infrastructure for university -based innovation and 
technology entrepreneurship. Research universities are connected to federal science funding, 
intellectual property systems, industry partnerships, venture capital markets,  incubators, 
accelerators, and entrepreneurship education programmes. This environment provides 
relatively structured pathways for STEM students and researchers to explore 
commercialisation.

because it allowed universities, small businesses, and nonprofit organisations to retain rights to

NSF I-Corps is one of the more visible examples of entrepreneurial STEM education in the 
United States. The programme focuses on helping researchers and students examine the 
commercial potential of research through customer discovery and entrepreneurial tr aining. It 
reflects a movement away from assuming that research novelty is sufficient for market 
adoption. Instead, research teams are encouraged to examine user needs, value propositions, 
and commercial pathways.

8. Proposed Framework for Entrepreneurial STEM Education 
The synthesis supports a six -dimensional framework for integrating business principles into 
STEM education. The framework includes curriculum integration, experiential learning, 
ecosystem partnerships, commercialisation infrastructure, faculty development,  and policy 
support. 
Curriculum integration refers to the embedding of business and entrepreneurship principles 
within STEM learning rather than treating entrepreneurship as an unrelated general course. This 
may involve in

within STEM learning rather than treating entrepreneurship as an unrelated general course. This 
may involve introducing market analysis into engineering design, inte llectual property into 
research methods, financial literacy into technology development, regulatory strategy into 
health innovation, and business model development into computer science or design projects. 
Integration should be progressive across educational levels. At earlier levels, learners may focus 
on creativity, problem identification, teamwork, and simple value creation. At higher levels, 
they may engage with prototypes, users, intellectual property, business models, and venture 
development.
